old: This puts the ester above the amide correctly but ranks ethyl acetate below the amide. Amides are the least reactive derivatives because N donates strongly and amide ion is a very poor leaving group.
new: This correctly makes the phenyl ester the most reactive but ranks ethyl acetate below the amide. Amides are the least reactive derivatives because N donates strongly and amide ion is a very poor leaving group.
why: c1 is II < III < I; the old text said it 'puts the ester above the amide correctly' and then that it ranks the ester below the amide (self-contradictory).

old: Losing a 43 u radical from m/z 100 gives m/z 57, not 58; that cleavage accounts for the separate m/z 57 and 43 peaks.
new: Any α-cleavage loses a radical and gives an odd-mass ion: losing 43 u from m/z 100 would give m/z 57, not 58. Cleavage on either side of the C=O gives the separate m/z 43 and 57 peaks.
why: Old x1 endorsed loss of a propyl radical, which B (no propyl on the C=O) cannot do; m/z 43 is CH3CO+ and 57 is C4H9+ from cleavage of the C(O)-isobutyl bond.

old: A terminal alkyne C–H (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) is acidic because of sp character, but the aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion is about a million times more stable.
new: A terminal alkyne C–H (pKa ≈ 25) is acidic because of sp character, but the C–H at b (pKa ≈ 16–18) is about 107–109 times more acidic, because its conjugate base is the aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion.
why: pKa 25 vs 16-18 is 7-9 units (10^7-10^9), not 'about a million'; compare acidity, not anion stability.
